question: What are the main causes of negative sentiment, and what specifically triggers them?

answer.answer_markdown:
**Negative sentiment is almost never about tone. It is about a decision nobody will explain, money that was taken and not returned, and a claim that stays denied after the customer has produced the evidence.**

The index is overwhelmingly negative: 23.5% of contacts are strongly negative and a further 61.6% negative, against 8.8% mildly positive and 2.5% strongly positive. Four causes carry most of that weight. Decisions denied or declined without explanation is the largest, on 1,171 contacts (21.6%). Fraud not stopped or not refunded is next, on 1,053 contacts (19.4%). Incorrect or conflicting information follows on 818 contacts (15.1%), and money held or not returned on 728 contacts (13.4%).

Each cause has a different home, which is where the operational trigger sits. Denied-without-explanation is a card and deposit-account problem: it attaches to 31.0% of credit card contacts and 26.3% of checking or savings contacts, but only 6.4% of the synthetic phone conversations. Fraud not stopped or not refunded is sharpest in payments: it attaches to 46.0% of money transfer and P2P contacts, 2.37 times the overall rate, against 26.9% of checking or savings contacts.

The largest negative theme names the trigger precisely: fraud and dispute claims denied despite evidence, 379 contacts (7.0% of the index) written 381 different ways across 41 states. The recorded root cause is that dispute teams apply rigid criteria and automated checks that never take in the evidence the customer supplied. The specific triggers repeat with unusual consistency: ATM claims closed without reconciling the cash cassettes or pulling the journal logs and footage, disputes refused on a misapplied filing deadline, and fraud claims rejected simply because a PIN or credential was used.

The angriest cause is the smallest one. Staff attitude or competence appears on only 287 contacts, but its mean sentiment is -1.54, worse than every other cause and well below the -1.26 of the largest. It is the multiplier rather than the cause: it turns a claim that was going to be denied anyway into a complaint about the bank itself.

quotes.quote: Chase denied the dispute, claiming the transaction was not eligible.
quotes.why: The largest cause in one line: a decision delivered with no reasoning the customer can test.

quotes.quote: I was told by the bank earlier that it had to be me because they generated a card stripe and they swiped the card instead of using the chip.
quotes.why: The fraud trigger: the bank's own evidence is used to put the loss back on the customer.

quotes.quote: Chase has placed an extended hold on these funds in my account.
quotes.why: Money held and not returned, the third cause, stated plainly.

quotes.quote: I was then told again that it was XXXX who decided to freeze my account, so I was transferred back to XXXX a second time and was told again that they at XXXX did not freeze my account and that Chase Bank has the final say concerning my account.
quotes.why: Conflicting information: two departments each naming the other as the one who froze the account.

quotes.quote: she came with a aggressive hostile tone and said you dont bank with us your employer does we dont need to cash your check bc we dont have to you bank with XXXX XXXX XXXX take your check there.
quotes.why: Staff attitude, the angriest cause: the smallest population but the strongest language.

caveats: The index mixes two corpora and every unfiltered number covers both: 4,425 real written CFPB complaints about one bank (July 2024 to June 2026) and 1,000 synthetic agent/customer phone conversations from September 2023. A complaint corpus is negative by construction, so the overall negative share describes this mix, not the bank's customer base.
Nearly all the positive sentiment in the index comes from the synthetic phone conversations rather than the complaints, so nothing here should be read as customers having become happier or unhappier.

The big negative causes are effectively complaints-only: of the 379 contacts in the largest negative theme, 378 are written complaints and 1 is a phone conversation, so the product splits above are complaint product splits.
Sentiment, driver categories and specific triggers are model-extracted per contact and a single contact can carry several at once, so the causes overlap and their shares do not sum to 100%.
followups: Of the fraud and dispute claims denied despite evidence, how many were later overturned, and how long did the reversal take?
Money transfer and P2P carries fraud-not-refunded at more than twice the overall rate: which flows drive it, wires, P2P sends or ACH pulls?
Staff attitude is the angriest cause: which contact reasons and which stage of a claim does it attach to most often?

confidence.badge: broad pattern · 4,511 calls · 25 months · 10 products · 53 states

SELECT key, COUNT(*) AS n_calls, SUM(CASE WHEN mn < 0 THEN -mn ELSE 0 END) AS mass, AVG(mn) AS mean_sentiment FROM (SELECT t.driver_category AS key, t.call_id, MIN(t.sentiment) AS mn, MAX(t.sentiment) AS mx FROM topics t JOIN calls c ON c.call_id = t.call_id WHERE 1=1 GROUP BY key, t.call_id) GROUP BY key HAVING n_calls >= ? AND mass > 0 ORDER BY mass DESC, key LIMIT ?

SELECT t.driver_category AS key, t.topic_id, t.call_id, t.sentiment, t.driver_category, t.driver FROM topics t JOIN calls c ON c.call_id = t.call_id WHERE 1=1 AND t.driver_category IN (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?) AND t.sentiment < 0
